food.text: Around 2,000 years ago, Bantu-speaking peoples arrived in southern Africa. They brought crop cultivation, animal husbandry and iron toolmaking with them, which changed how people in the region produced their food.
The Bantu-speakers who settled southern Africa grew grain crops extensively and raised cattle, sheep and goats. They also grew pumpkins, beans and leafy greens as vegetables.
Not everyone in southern Africa farmed. The San hunted wild animals and gathered wild tubers and vegetables, while the Khoi-Khoi ate meat and milk. What people ate helped define who they were.

The Bantu-speakers of southern Africa ate dishes of grain, meat, milk and vegetables. They also ate fermented grain and fermented milk products, so preserving and transforming food through fermentation was part of their diet.
Both the Khoisan and the Bantu traditionally ate roasted meat. They also dried meat so that it could be kept and eaten later.

The earliest archaeological evidence in the Kongo region comes from Tchissanga, a site dated to about 600 BCE, though it does not prove which ethnic group lived there. The Kongo people had settled the area well before the fifth century CE, and they used its rich resources and developed farming methods.

According to James Denbow, the society that used the rich resources and farming methods of the Kongo region had probably achieved social complexity by the second century CE. Farming and the use of local resources came to support more complex communities.

art.text: The Sao civilization flourished from about the 6th century BCE beside the Chari River, south of Lake Chad. Its artifacts show that the Sao were skilled workers in bronze, copper and iron.

The cultures of Central Africa show many similarities in music, dance, art and body adornment. The source links this to common historical processes and widespread population movements. Many of these practices stem from shared origins as largely Nilo-Saharan or Bantu peoples.
In southeast Zimbabwe, early Bantu-speaking farmers made Iron Age pottery of the Silver Leaves or Matola tradition. It dates to the third to fifth centuries AD.

Sao finds include bronze sculptures, terra cotta statues of human and animal figures, coins, funerary urns, household utensils, jewelry, highly decorated pottery, and spears. The largest Sao archaeological finds have been made south of Lake Chad.

Sao archaeological finds include bronze sculptures and terra cotta statues of human and animal figures. Sao sites have also yielded funerary urns, jewelry and highly decorated pottery. The largest Sao finds have been made south of Lake Chad.

The Sao are the earliest people to have left clear traces of their presence in the territory of modern Cameroon. Several ethnic groups of northern Cameroon and southern Chad, particularly the Sara people, claim descent from them.

More numerous in Zimbabwe were the makers of Ziwa and Gokomere ceramic wares, dating to the fourth century AD. Imported beads have been found at Gokomere and Ziwa sites, possibly received in return for gold exported to the coast.

The Silver Leaves or Matola pottery tradition belonged to the eastern stream of Bantu expansion, sometimes called Kwale. That stream began west of the Great Lakes, reached southeastern Kenya and northeastern Tanzania, then went south to Mozambique, southeastern Zimbabwe and Natal.

literature.text: Bantu peoples across Central and Southern Africa preserved their culture without writing. Instead, their traditions were oral, passed down through folk tales, songs, and festivals from one generation to the next.
In Bantu oral fables, the hare was the central character, celebrated as a symbol of skill and cunning. Its main rival was the hyena, portrayed as sneaky and deceptive.

Bantu oral tradition held that kings and heroes could live on for centuries simply by being remembered and retold in stories. In contrast, the spirits of ordinary people were believed to fade away after only a few generations.
In these fables, the lion and the elephant typically stood for brute force rather than cleverness. They served as foils to sharper-witted characters like the hare in Bantu storytelling.
Bantu storytellers considered the turtle even craftier than the hare. Rather than relying on speed or strength, the turtle was said to defeat its rivals through patience and strong will.

Along the Congo River, where the hare was not part of local wildlife, storytellers gave its clever role to the antelope instead. This shows how the same fable adapted to different regions within the Bantu world.

In Sotho culture, the hare was replaced as the clever hero by the jackal, a shift thought to reflect neighboring Khoisan influence. Among the Khoisan, the jackal symbolized astuteness while the hare was seen as foolish.

Among the Zulu, storytellers told hare tales like other Bantu peoples, but in some versions the ferret took over as the clever hero instead. This variation shows the flexibility of the widespread Bantu fable tradition.

science.text: The Sao civilization flourished in northern Central Africa from about the 6th century BCE, living by the Chari River south of Lake Chad. Sao artifacts show that they were skilled workers in bronze, copper, and iron.

The first Bantu-speaking farmers reached what is now Zimbabwe around 2,000 years ago. They made early Iron Age pottery, including the Silver Leaves or Matola tradition of the third to fifth centuries AD, found in southeast Zimbabwe.

Archaeological evidence clearly indicates that from the first century BCE, iron working and cereal farming of millet and sorghum spread south together from southern Tanzania and northern Zambia. By the third or fourth century CE they had reached the eastern Cape region of South Africa. It seems highly probable that this happened through the migrations of Bantu-speaking peoples.
The Bantu expansion spread iron technology to Eastern and Southern Africa between 500 BCE and 400 CE. This spread is shown in the Urewe culture.

The Urewe culture grew up around Lake Victoria during the Early Iron Age, with sites dating from the 5th century BC to the 6th century AD. It is recognised as the first Iron Age community to reach Southern Africa, and its pots and smelting furnaces are key evidence of early ironworking.

More substantial in numbers in Zimbabwe were the makers of the Ziwa and Gokomere ceramic wares, dating to the fourth century AD. Their early Iron Age tradition belonged to the highlands facies, which moved inland to Malawi and Zimbabwe.

Two branches of the Urewe tradition carried ironworking south. Pioneers of the Kwale branch, which followed the eastern coast, reached KwaZulu-Natal between 200 and 300 AD. The Nkope branch ran from southern Tanzania through Malawi and eastern Zambia into Zimbabwe, and reached Limpopo Province by 400 AD.

Scholars disagree about where the Bantu words for ironworking came from. Christopher Ehret argues they were borrowed from Central Sudanic languages near modern Uganda and Kenya. Jan Vansina argues instead that they originated in non-Bantu languages in Nigeria, and that the technology then spread south and east.

Researchers studying Urewe iron production have identified tree species from the charcoal in smelting furnaces and open hearths. They combined this with pollen analyses of peat bogs to reconstruct the environment. The settlement period fits a cooling and drying phase around 1000 BC.

culture.text: In the first millennium BCE, two dominant San groups lived across Southern Africa. The Tshua San spread across present-day Botswana, Zimbabwe and Zambia and occupied the Shashe-Limpopo basin, while the Khwe San lived further west across Botswana, Namibia, Angola and Zambia.

The name San comes from a Khoekhoe word meaning 'those who pick things up from the ground,' used for foraging hunter-gatherers who did not own livestock. This distinguished them from pastoralist Khoekhoe and agricultural communities living nearby in Southern Africa.

One stream of Bantu-speaking migrants, called the Western Stream, moved south along the Atlantic coast and by river through the Congo rainforest. They reached central Angola by around 500 BCE as part of the wider Bantu expansion into Central Africa.
The earliest known inhabitants of present-day Zimbabwe were the San people. About 2,000 years ago, Bantu-speaking peoples settled in the region.

The Khoekhoe were pastoralists who may have arrived in Southern Africa during the Late Stone Age. They were possibly displaced from parts of their territory when the Bantu expansion reached the area roughly 1,500 to 2,000 years ago.

Pioneering Bantu-speaking groups reached what is now KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa by 300 CE, moving along the coast. They reached the modern Limpopo Province by 500 CE, as the Bantu expansion reached South Africa.

From the 4th century CE, communities of the Gokomere culture near Great Zimbabwe farmed the valley and mined and worked iron, though they built no stone structures. These were among the area's earliest Iron Age settlements.

The Bantu expansion decimated the Khoisan, who had been much more widespread than they are today, and their modern distribution is a result of that decimation. The Khoisan also mingled considerably with Bantu-speaking groups. Evidence of this survives in the click phonemes found in many Southern African Bantu languages, including Xhosa.

The Silver Leaves or Matola tradition was part of the eastern stream of the Bantu expansion, sometimes called Kwale. It originated west of the Great Lakes, spread to southeastern Kenya and northeastern Tanzania, then went south to Mozambique, southeastern Zimbabwe and Natal.

The San presence in this era is especially evident in the Tsodilo Hills region of northern Botswana, where the Tshua and Khwe San groups encountered migrant herder groups and herder-farmers during the Bantu expansion (2000 BCE–1000 CE). In this process, the San were partly driven off their ancestral lands or incorporated by Bantu-speaking groups.
